translationSpecificSourceLines.old: What gives *agapē* its specifically Christian content is not the word itself but Christ’s use of it — and the way the New Testament writers fill the word with the content of Christ’s own life and death. When John writes “God is love” (1 John 4:8, 16, NET), he uses *agapē*; the content of that statement is what God has done in Christ. When Paul writes the great love chapter (1 Corinthians 13), he is describing the kind of love that Christ exhibited in His life and death. When the love commands appear (love God, love neighbor, love enemies, love one another), the love being commanded is the love Christ has shown — the kind that does specifically what Christ did.

*The purchase has ethical consequences.* “glorify God with your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20, NET). “Do not become slaves of men” (1 Corinthians 7:23, NET). The believer who has been bought is freed *from* old slaveries and freed *for* God's service. This is the practical theology of Christian freedom.

First, Christ as "the Amen." *Ho Amēn* — "the Amen." Christ is here given the title "the Amen." This draws on the Old Testament's “the faithful God” (Isaiah 65:16, NET) — the God who is firm, reliable, true. Christ is the Amen — the embodiment of God's firmness, reliability, and truth. He is not merely the one who says "amen"; He is the Amen Himself. In Him, the firmness and certainty that "amen" affirms is personally embodied.

*The legalistic reduction.* The opposite error. *Anomia* is read as violation of specific external commandments only — particular acts of misconduct that can be enumerated and avoided. Missing this view is the deeper dispositional and structural dimension of *anomia*. The Pharisees of the gospels were not antinomians; they were precisely legalists — and Christ called them “full of hypocrisy and lawlessness” (Matthew 23:28, NET). Their *anomia* was hidden in their fastidious legalism. The Lutheran reading of sin requires the dispositional and structural dimensions, not just the catalog of forbidden acts.

*Human being, generic.* The dominant usage. “For what benefit is it for a person to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his life?…” (Mark 8:36, NET) — *anthrōpos*, any human being. “A man came, sent from God, whose name was John” (John 1:6, NET) — *anthrōpos*. Most of the New Testament's *anthrōpoi* are simply people.
*A particular person.* “There was a man named Joseph” (Luke 23:50, NET). The word for "person" or "individual" when no specifier is needed.
*A man as opposed to God.* “what is highly prized among men is utterly detestable in God’s sight” (Luke 16:15, NET). The *anthrōpos*-side of the human-divine contrast.

This text gives the structural framework for the entire Pauline doctrine of salvation. Romans 5:12-21 elaborates: “consequently, just as condemnation for all people came through one transgression, so too through the one righteous act came righteousness leading to life for all people” (Romans 5:18, NET). The parallel is exact. As Adam's act involves all who are in him, so Christ's act involves all who are in Him. The work of the gospel is to transfer the *anthrōpos* from one head to the other.

*Docetism.* The ancient heresy that taught Christ only seemed to be human — that His humanity was an appearance, a phantom, a mask over His divine reality. The first generation of Christians was already correcting it: “every spirit that confesses Jesus as the Christ who has come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:2, NET). Docetism survives in popular Christian preaching that emphasizes Christ’s divinity to the exclusion of His humanity. When Christ’s hunger, tiredness, sorrow, or weakness are treated as performances or strategic accommodations rather than real human experiences, Docetism is at work. The New Testament’s *anthrōpos* applied to Christ is decisive against this: He was tired (John 4:6), He hungered (Matthew 4:2), He wept (John 11:35), He died (Mark 15:37). All of these were actual experiences of an actual *anthrōpos*.

Then, after the resurrection, the same Twelve receive a new designation. They are no longer just *mathētai*. They are *apostoloi* — apostles, ones sent. The risen Christ commissions them: “as the Father has sent me, I also send you” (John 20:21, NET). What had been a relationship of being-taught becomes also a relationship of being-sent. The pupil becomes the messenger. The student becomes the foundation of the church the Master is building.

*Matthew 10:1-5 / Mark 3:13-19 / Luke 6:12-16 (the appointment of the Twelve).* “Jesus called his 12 disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits so they could cast them out and heal every kind of disease and sickness. Now these are the names of the 12 apostles: first, Simon (called Peter), and Andrew his brother; James son of Zebedee and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him” (Matthew 10:1-4, NET). The Greek of verse 2: *tōn de dōdeka apostolōn ta onomata estin tauta*.

*Origin or source.* Closely related to the temporal sense but emphasizing causation rather than chronology. Christ as the *archē* of creation (Colossians 1:18) is the source from which creation comes, not just the first item in a sequence. The “the originator of God’s creation” (Revelation 3:14, NET) similarly names Christ as the origin of the creating work, not as the first thing created.

This is the Pauline doctrine of Christ's cosmic exaltation. After His resurrection and ascension, Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father, with all spiritual powers subordinated to His authority. The four-word list is not exhaustive; Paul is naming the major categories of cosmic authority in the religious vocabulary of his time. Whatever powers exist — angelic, demonic, political, spiritual — all of them are under Christ. The believer who is in Christ shares in this exaltation, since “seated us together with him in the heavenly realms” (Ephesians 2:6, NET).

The Lutheran position is consistent with the broader Reformation pattern of taking the New Testament’s grammar at face value. Paul says “the bread that we break” (1 Cor 10:16, NET). The bread is being broken. It is still bread. Paul says “this bread” (1 Cor 11:26–28, NET) eight times across five verses, after the consecration, after the participation in the body. The bread is bread. If Paul thought the bread had become something other than bread, he would have said so. The same pattern appears at Emmaus (Luke 24:30, 35) and throughout Acts (2:42, 46; 20:7, 11). The breaking of bread is the breaking of bread. The Lord is given in it. The substance does not change. The Word does the work.

The first is Roman Catholic transubstantiation — the bread no longer being bread. The Lutheran response: Scripture continues to call it bread after consecration; “this bread” (1 Cor 11:26–28, NET); the substance does not change; the Aristotelian metaphysics required to defend the doctrine are not what the New Testament teaches. The Lutheran *sacramental union* preserves both the bread and the body, without making either disappear into the other.

*To exercise authority over — neutral.* On this reading *authentein* describes the ordinary exercise of authority, carrying no built-in judgment about whether the authority is legitimately held or well used. The clause then prohibits a woman from teaching and from exercising authority over a man, full stop, without any implied "improperly." This is the reading of most modern English translations (NASB, CSB, NET, and — in a deliberately ambiguous rendering — the NIV's "assume authority"). Its main support: several of the surviving occurrences are plainly neutral or even positive, and a negative sense has to be read in from context rather than found in the word.
“And this prefigured baptism, which now saves you—not the washing off of physical dirt but the pledge of a good conscience to God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,…” (1 Peter 3:21, NET)

First, baptism actually does what the New Testament says it does. The Lutheran tradition reads the baptism passages straightforwardly, without translating them into figurative or symbolic categories. When Peter says baptism saves (1 Pet 3:21), it saves. When Paul says we were baptized into Christ's death (Rom 6:3), we were. When the Lord says we must be born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5), the water and the Spirit together accomplish the new birth. When Titus 3:5 calls baptism “he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit,” baptism is the washing of regeneration. When Ananias tells Paul to “be baptized, and have your sins washed away” (Acts 22:16, NET), baptism washes away sins. The verbs are not decorative.

Second, baptism is for infants too. The confessional Lutheran position affirms infant baptism on several converging grounds. The Great Commission says “make disciples of all nations, baptizing them” (Matt 28:19, NET), without age restriction. Acts 2:39 declares “For the promise is for you and your children, and for all who are far away, as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.” Household baptisms in Acts — Lydia (Acts 16:15), the Philippian jailer's whole household (16:33), Cornelius and his household (10:48), Crispus's household (18:8), Stephanas's household (1 Cor 1:16) — include dependents without recorded individual professions, in a culture where households included infants and young children. Colossians 2:11–12 explicitly connects baptism to circumcision, which was administered to infant boys on the eighth day. Mark 10:13–16 records Jesus's welcome of children: “the kingdom of God belongs to such as these”

When Jesus began His public ministry, His message had a center. Mark summarizes it: “He said, ‘The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe the gospel!’” (Mark 1:15, NET). The kingdom of God was the heart of Jesus's proclamation. He preached it, taught it in parables, demonstrated it in His miracles, and made it the subject of the prayer He taught His disciples: "Thy kingdom come."

This entry is about that word — *basileia* — and about the reign of God that is central to Jesus's proclamation and to the believer's hope. The [Klēronomos](/greek/kleronomos/) entry names the believer as heir; the kingdom is central to the inheritance the believer receives. The believer who has been made an heir of God will “inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34, NET).

The kingdom is *already* present. In the person and ministry of Jesus, the reign of God broke into history. In the preaching of the gospel and the administration of the Sacraments, the kingdom continues to come. The believer who is in Christ has already been “transferred us to the kingdom of the Son he loves” (Colossians 1:13, NET). The kingdom is a present reality, hidden but real, recognized by faith.

*The reduction of the kingdom to an earthly political project.* Some Christianity, in various forms (Christian nationalism, dominionism, certain forms of the social gospel), has effectively reduced the kingdom of God to an earthly political or social program — implying that the kingdom is built through political power, cultural transformation, or social reform. The biblical pattern refuses this. Christ’s kingdom is “not from this world” (John 18:36, NET). The kingdom comes through the gospel, not through political power. The believer’s engagement in the temporal realm is real and important, but it is not the building of God’s kingdom.

This particular *bēma* has a connection to the New Testament. In Acts 18, during Paul's eighteen-month stay in Corinth, the Jewish community brought him before the Roman proconsul Gallio “the judgment seat” (Acts 18:12, NET) — *epi to bēma*. Paul stood before this very platform, or one very much like it, accused by his opponents. Gallio dismissed the case, declining to rule on what he regarded as an internal Jewish religious dispute. But the scene is vivid: Paul, the accused, standing before the raised tribunal where the magistrate sat in judgment.

A few years later, Paul wrote to the Corinthians: “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10, NET). The word he used was *bēma*. The Corinthians, reading this, would not have thought of an abstract theological concept. They would have pictured the actual *bēma* in their own marketplace — the raised stone platform where Gallio had sat, where Paul himself had stood accused, where verdicts were rendered and consequences assigned. Paul was telling them: there is a *bēma* greater than the one in your marketplace. Christ Himself sits on it. And every one of us — Paul included — will stand before it.

Biblical *chara* — the Greek word the New Testament uses — is something else. The chained Paul, facing execution, rejoiced. The Christ who endured the cross did so “for the joy set out for him” (Hebrews 12:2, NET). The disciples in Acts, beaten and ordered not to preach, “so they left the council rejoicing because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name” (Acts 5:41, NET). Joy in the New Testament is not the circumstance-dependent happiness of English usage; it is a substantive disposition grounded in something more durable than circumstances.

*The* *“**if you really had faith you would be joyful all the time**”* *pressure.* A particular form of the previous error. Some Christianity has treated continuing sorrow, lament, or non-cheerful feeling as evidence of inadequate faith. The biblical pattern refuses this. The psalmists lament extensively while remaining in faith. Christ wept at Lazarus’s tomb. Paul says he is “sorrowful, but always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10, NET). The believer’s joy and the believer’s sorrow can coexist; the absence of cheerful feeling does not indicate the absence of biblical *chara*.

The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: address the joy-versus-happiness confusion, which the entry’s opening has already exposed through the prisoner who wrote the most joy-saturated letter in the New Testament. Your students likely associate “joy” with happiness — circumstance-dependent positive feeling. Biblical *chara* is something else: grounded in Christ, in His person and work and the believer’s union with Him; the circumstances may shift, but the source does not. That is the framework to hand them — and the joy-suffering paradox runs straight through the New Testament: Peter writes to persecuted believers of joy that is inexpressible (1 Peter 1:6-8); Paul is “sorrowful, but always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10, NET). Biblical joy does not require the absence of suffering; it operates within it.
The Son is called “the representation of his essence” (Hebrews 1:3, NET). *Representation* renders *charaktēr*; *essence* renders [hypostasis](/greek/hypostasis/).
“And if it is by grace, it is no longer by works, otherwise grace would no longer be grace.” (Romans 11:6, NET)
- The whole sphere of being a recipient of favor — “this grace in which we stand” (Rom 5:2, NET), the state of being in grace.

- A messiah — the more general sense of one who is anointed. Used a few times in eschatological warnings about false messiahs. “For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will mislead many” (Matt 24:5, NET).

The corresponding clause concerns release. The NET represents the future perfect construction with *will have been bound*. That form deserves attention, but the grammar should not be made to establish an independent heavenly endorsement of every church decision.

Phoebe. Paul calls her *diakonos* — the masculine form of the noun, applied to her as a title. The verse is famously contested. Translations vary: “servant” (NET, KJV) and “deacon” (NIV, NRSV) are both standard. The Greek does not distinguish, but the use of the masculine title-form *diakonos* (rather than the feminine adjective “serving”) strongly suggests a formal office or recognized role, not merely the general sense of “one who serves.” Paul also calls her *prostatis* — “patron” — indicating that she had substantial social standing and provided significant material support to Paul and to other Christians. Whatever the precise nature of her office, Phoebe was a *diakonos* of the church at Cenchreae, and Paul commends her to the Roman believers in language that names her by this title.

It is also the word Jesus used the night before He died, when He took the cup at the Last Supper and said: “this is my blood, the blood of the covenant” (Matt 26:28, NET). Or, as Paul preserves the saying: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (1 Cor 11:25, NET). The Greek word behind "covenant" in those words of institution is *diathēkē* — the same word that gives your Bible its name.

The image is more apt than it may first appear. False doctrine is not just an intellectual mistake; it is a spiritual disease. It infects the hearer; it spreads through the community; it produces specific symptoms — anxiety where there should be assurance, legalism where there should be freedom, doubt where there should be confidence, despair where there should be hope. The Pastoral Epistles are full of warnings about teachers whose doctrine is making the church sick: those who “some have strayed from these and turned away to empty discussion” (1 Timothy 1:6, NET), those who teach “spreads false teachings” (1 Timothy 6:3, NET), those whose teaching “like gangrene” (2 Timothy 2:17, NET).

Sound doctrine, by contrast, is medicine. It nourishes the hearer; it strengthens the believer's faith; it produces the kind of life that fits with the gospel. Titus 2 develops this dimension extensively: the various groups in the church — older men, older women, younger women, younger men, slaves — are each to live in ways that “the teaching of God our Savior” (Titus 2:10, NET). The doctrine and the life work together. Healthy teaching produces healthy living; healthy living adorns the doctrine that produced it.
- To vindicate, to prove right. “wisdom is vindicated by her deeds” (Matt 11:19, NET) — wisdom is shown to be right by what it does. Same verb, “vindication” register.

In ordinary first-century Greek, an *eikōn* could be many things: a portrait, a statue, the image of an emperor stamped on a coin, the likeness of one person reflected in another. When Jesus asks “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?” (Mark 12:16, NET), He is using the everyday sense. Caesar’s face is on the coin. That is the *eikōn*.
- The image to which humans are being conformed. “Predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom 8:29, NET).

The image is also your destiny. Romans 8:29 says we are predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son. The arc of the Christian life is image-restoration — the slow remaking, through union with Christ and through the means of grace, of what we lost in Adam. We will not finish this work in this life. We will finish it in the resurrection, when “we will be like him because we will see him just as he is” (1 John 3:2, NET). But the work has begun, and the One it conforms us to is the One in whose image we were made.

The Greek *eirēnē* inherits this whole range. When the New Testament says the believer has *eirēnē* with God (Romans 5:1), the meaning is not narrowly that hostility has ceased but comprehensively that the believer has been brought into the wholeness of relationship with God that the *shalom* tradition names. When Christ says “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27, NET), He is not giving an absence of trouble — He is giving the substantial well-being that belongs to His own life with the Father, now offered to those who follow Him.

This is the inheritance the apostles draw on. When Jesus tells Peter, “on this rock I will build my church” (Matt 16:18, NET), He is not coining a new term. He is invoking the entire Septuagint history of *qahal Yahweh* — the assembly of God’s people — and locating Himself at its center as the one who will build it. The *ekklēsia* He builds is in continuity with the *qahal* of Israel and in fulfillment of God’s purposes for a gathered covenant people.

*The antinomian misreading.* The classic counterpart of the libertarian reduction. The Christian is free from the law; therefore the Christian has no obligation to live according to the law. The Galatian situation was the first version of this temptation, and the Pauline response is direct: “For you were called to freedom, brothers and sisters; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity to indulge your flesh, but through love serve one another” (Galatians 5:13, NET). Lutheran teaching has consistently opposed antinomianism — most famously in the antinomian controversies of the 1530s and 1540s, which produced the Formula of Concord’s careful treatment of the law’s three uses.

The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: teach the distinction between English “hope” and biblical *elpis*. In everyday English, *hope* names an uncertain wish — *I hope it doesn’t rain; I hope I get the job*. The Greek *elpis* names confident expectation: the believer’s hope is grounded in God’s promise, secured by Christ’s completed work, sealed by the Spirit. The distinction is pastorally important. When your students read “in hope we were saved” (Romans 8:24, NET), they need to know it does not mean “saved by wishful thinking” but “saved into the confident expectation of what God has promised.” The Old Testament models it: “this I call to mind; therefore I have hope...The Lord’s loyal kindness never ceases” (Lamentations 3:21-24, NET) — hope grounded in God’s character, not in the visible situation.
“Give us today our daily bread,” (Matthew 6:11, NET)
“Give us each day our daily bread.” (Luke 11:3, NET)

Luke’s version follows a disciple’s request: “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples” (Luke 11:1, NET). The petition reads, “Give us each day our daily bread” (Luke 11:3, NET). Luke uses the present imperative *didou*, while Matthew uses the aorist *dos*. Luke’s wording emphasizes the repeated daily asking; Matthew 6:11 asks for today’s bread. Both use *epiousios* and express dependence on the Father’s provision.

Third, Christ Himself is the chief *episkopos* — “the shepherd and guardian of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25, NET). The human pastor’s oversight is derivative and ministerial; the ultimate oversight belongs to Christ. This shapes how Lutheran theology understands what the pastor does.

Paul writes: “For we consider that a person is declared righteous by faith apart from the works of the law” (Romans 3:28, NET). And again: “for no one is declared righteous before him by the works of the law, for through the law comes the knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20, NET). And again: “yet we know that no one is justified by the works of the law but by the faithfulness of Jesus Christ...because by the works of the law no one will be justified” (Galatians 2:16, NET). The Pauline statement is consistent and emphatic. Justification before God is not by works.

James writes: “What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but does not have works? Can this kind of faith save him...So also faith, if it does not have works, is dead...You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone...For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so also faith without works is dead” (James 2:14-26, NET). The Jacobean statement is equally consistent and emphatic. Faith without works does not save.

The Septuagint background is substantial. *Ergon* in the LXX translates several Hebrew terms for work, deed, and accomplishment, most commonly *ma'aseh* (work, deed, action) and *melakah* (work, occupation, business). The Old Testament's view of work is consistent and substantive. Work is part of the creation order — Adam was placed in the garden “to care for it and to maintain it” (Genesis 2:15, NET) before the fall. The fall corrupts work (Genesis 3:17-19 — work becomes toil), but does not eliminate it. The Sabbath establishes a rhythm of work and rest. The various commandments concerning work (the seventh-year fallow, the Year of Jubilee, the laws on hired labor) regulate work in ways that recognize both its dignity and its dangers.

First, the James context is the orthodox-claim-without-fruit problem. James is addressing those who claim faith but produce no evidence of it in their lives — “If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, keep warm and eat well,’ but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is it?” (James 2:15-16, NET). The problem James is addressing is the dead orthodoxy that affirms doctrinal content without producing the kind of life the doctrine should produce.

The Cornelius episode is the New Testament's most extended treatment of the inclusion of Gentiles in the people of God. Peter receives a vision of unclean animals and is commanded to eat. He resists; he is told three times not to call common what God has cleansed. Then he is sent to the household of Cornelius, a Roman centurion who has been praying and giving alms. Peter preaches the gospel to Cornelius's household; the Holy Spirit falls on them; they speak in tongues; Peter recognizes the Gentile inclusion and baptizes them. He then has to defend the action to the Jerusalem church (Acts 11), arguing that “therefore if God gave them the same gift as he also gave us after believing in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to hinder God?” (Acts 11:17, NET).

*Revelation 5:9 and 7:9.* “They were singing a new song: ‘You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals because you were killed, and at the cost of your own blood you have purchased for God persons from every tribe, language, people, and nation’” (Revelation 5:9, NET). “After these things I looked, and here was an enormous crowd that no one could count, made up of persons from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne and before the Lamb dressed in long white robes, and with palm branches in their hands” (Revelation 7:9, NET). The Greek of 5:9: *ek pasēs phylēs kai glōssēs kai laou kai ethnous*.

When Mark opens his Gospel by writing “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark 1:1, NET), he is taking a word that every Greek-speaking person in the empire would have associated with imperial announcement and applying it to a Galilean carpenter executed by Roman authority. The word choice is a claim. The real good news is not about Caesar. The real good news is about Jesus.

Luke 2:14 requires a textual distinction. Some manuscripts read the nominative *eudokia*; others have the genitive *eudokias*, differing by a final sigma. The NET follows the genitive and speaks of peace among people with whom God is pleased. The sense is his favor toward them, not peace earned by their goodwill.

*The conditional blessing misreading.* Some traditions have made the believer’s blessing conditional on his ongoing obedience or faithfulness. The believer who falls into sin or struggles with doubt is treated as having lost the blessing until he restores his standing through repentance and improved performance. The Pauline doctrine is more secure. The blessing is “in Christ” (Ephesians 1:3, NET) — it rests on the believer’s union with Christ, not on his continuing performance. The believer who is in Christ remains blessed even in the moments of sin and weakness; his task is to receive forgiveness and continue in the blessing he has been given.

The sentence follows a claim of permission that the NET places within quotation marks. Its notes understand Paul to be repeating Corinthian slogans and correcting their misuse. This is a contextual interpretation, not something proved by the verb or by quotation marks supplied in an English edition.
“To all those loved by God in Rome, called to be saints” (Romans 1:7, NET)
“to the church of God that is in Corinth, to those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, and called to be saints” (1 Corinthians 1:2, NET)
“to the saints [in Ephesus], the faithful in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 1:1, NET)
“to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi” (Philippians 1:1, NET)
“to the saints, the faithful brothers and sisters in Christ, at Colossae” (Colossians 1:2, NET)

“for the life of every living thing is in the blood. So I myself have assigned it to you on the altar to make atonement for your lives, for the blood makes atonement by means of the life.” (Leviticus 17:11, NET)

One specific application matters here that the [Sōma](/greek/soma/) entry did not develop. The medieval Roman practice of withholding the cup from the laity — offering only the bread to communicants, with the priest receiving both elements at the altar — was one of the practices the Lutheran Reformation rejected with particular vigor. The Latin term for the medieval restriction was *communio sub una specie* (communion in one kind only). Christ instituted communion in *both* kinds — bread and cup — and commanded “drink from it, all of you” (Matt 26:27, NET). The Lutheran insistence on *communio sub utraque specie* (communion in both kinds, bread and cup, for all communicants) was a return to the practice Christ commanded. Contemporary Roman Catholic practice has substantially restored the cup to the laity in many settings, but the historical Reformation dispute was substantive, and the Lutheran restoration of the cup is one of the practices the Lutheran tradition has retained without revisitation.
- A specific wrong act. One sin, one occurrence. “everyone who practices sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34, NET).

- Sin as a power. This is the one English readers most often miss. In Romans especially, Paul personifies *hamartia* as an active agent. It “sin reigned in death” (Rom 5:21, NET), it "dwells in" people (Rom 7:17), it “produced death in me” (Rom 7:13, NET). Paul writes about sin the way a doctor writes about a disease that is not just present but actively at work.
- The guilt and burden of sin — the weight that has to be taken away. “the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29, NET).

Here is something your English Bible cannot easily show you. When Paul writes about sin as a power, he very often puts the definite article in front of it — *hē hamartia*, “the Sin,” the way you would name a person or a country. English has no graceful way to carry that. “The sin came into the world” sounds like a typo, so translators quietly drop the article and print “sin entered the world” (Romans 5:12, NET). But the article is doing real work. Paul is not talking about your sins, plural, the items on the list. He is talking about Sin, singular — a power that got loose in the world through one man and has been running the place ever since. Read Romans 5 through 7 watching for that little word *hē*, and a character walks onto the stage: Sin enters, reigns, seizes territory, deceives, pays wages, kills. It is the difference between reading a police blotter and reading about an occupying army.

The NET retains the grasping language. Other translations make the sense of exploitation explicit. Either way, the passage should not be reduced to a dictionary entry with a doctrine attached afterward.

First, the wrath of God against sin is real, and the cross is where it fell. This is one of the doctrines that contemporary American Christianity has most quietly abandoned. Many sermons, many books, many pastoral conversations now speak of God’s love without speaking of God’s wrath, as if the two were alternatives rather than the consistent twin emphasis of Scripture. They are not alternatives. Paul opens Romans by announcing that “for the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth by their unrighteousness,” (Rom 1:18, NET), and he builds toward Romans 3:25 by establishing that this wrath is real and that all humans, Jew and Gentile, deserve it.

The second is denying the wrath of God altogether. This is the move that modern liberal Protestant theology made most decisively in the twentieth century, and that many evangelical Christians have quietly absorbed since. God is love, the move runs; God’s wrath is a primitive misreading; God could not be angry at His creatures and still be the God of the New Testament. The biblical evidence pushes back hard. The wrath of God is mentioned more often in the New Testament than in the Old, in fact. The Lord Jesus Himself spoke of the coming wrath repeatedly. The book of Revelation describes “the wrath of the Lamb” (Rev 6:16, NET) — Christ Himself executing divine judgment. The doctrine of propitiation depends on the wrath being real. Deny the wrath, and the cross becomes hard to make sense of. What was Christ accomplishing if not the propitiation His own apostle named?

Second, confession is public and corporate, not private only. The New Testament’s consistent emphasis on “before people” (Matt 10:32–33, NET), “with your mouth” (Rom 10:9–10, NET), “in the presence of many witnesses” (1 Tim 6:12, NET) refuses the merely interior model of Christian faith. The faith that has not broken into speech is incomplete on Paul’s grammar. The believer is to confess Christ before others, to say back what the church has heard, to join the corporate “we believe” of the historic creeds.

The verse is theologically important because it grounds the New Testament's adoption doctrine in Old Testament typology. Israel as God's “my son, my firstborn” (Exodus 4:22, NET) is the original *huiothesia* in salvation history. The believer in Christ — Jew or Gentile — participates in the same kind of relationship that God established with Israel, scaled up through the work of Christ. The continuity between the testaments is preserved (Israel's *huiothesia* is real and continues to belong to Israel); the universalization in Christ extends the *huiothesia* to all who believe.

*Negative spiritual sonship.* “the people of the evil one” (Matthew 13:38, NET). “you son of the devil” (Acts 13:10 — Paul's rebuke of Elymas). The same lexical structure used to name the spiritual paternity of those opposed to God.

*Romans 1:5 and 16:26.* “Through him we have received grace and our apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles on behalf of his name” (Romans 1:5, NET). “but now is disclosed, and through the prophetic scriptures has been made known to all the nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—” (Romans 16:26, NET). The Greek of both: *eis hypakoēn pisteōs*.

*Psalm 40:1* — “I relied completely on the Lord, and he turned toward me and heard my cry for help.” The Hebrew *qavoh qiviti* repeats the verb for waiting to intensify it. The NET expresses the resulting confidence as complete reliance on the Lord. This is active, expectant waiting, directed toward the God who hears.

The book of Job is the Old Testament's extended treatment of patient endurance under inexplicable suffering. Job loses his children, his wealth, his health, and his community standing. His wife counsels him to “curse God and die” (Job 2:9, NET). His friends increase his suffering by their misguided counsel. Throughout the book Job questions, complains, and demands answers from God — but Job does not curse God, does not abandon his integrity, does not move from his fundamental confession that the LORD is God and that he is God's. The book of Job is the Old Testament's central treatment of *hypomonē*.

*The reduction of the name to historical reference.* Some critical scholarship treats “Jesus” as merely the personal name of the historical man, with all the divine and theological weight added by the church later through what is sometimes called the “Christ of faith” overlay. The New Testament will not bear this reduction. The name itself was given with theological content from the beginning — “she will give birth to a son and you will name him Jesus because he will save his people from their sins.” (Matthew 1:21, NET). The mission is named with the name. The “Jesus of history” and the “Christ of faith” distinction collapses at the point of the angelic naming: this Jesus is from the start the one who saves; the historical figure and the theological figure are the same Person with the same name.
“For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, how much more, since we have been reconciled, will we be saved by his life?” (Romans 5:10, NET)
- The cosmic reconciliation that includes “things on earth or things in heaven” (Col 1:20, NET).

The third is universalism — the inference from “in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor 5:19, NET) that all individuals will ultimately be saved regardless of faith. Paul’s own grammar refuses the inference. The same passage that announces cosmic reconciliation also issues the apostolic appeal: “We plead with you on Christ’s behalf, ‘Be reconciled to God!’” (2 Cor 5:20, NET). The appeal would be unnecessary if the cosmic reconciliation automatically secured every individual’s salvation. The New Testament’s pattern is that the objective work of reconciliation has been accomplished for the world (universally, through the cross), and the subjective reception of that reconciliation comes through faith. The two are not the same. Confessional Lutheran theology has consistently held both: Christ died for all (objective universal accomplishment) and the saving benefit is received by faith (subjective particular reception). Universalism collapses the second into the first; particular redemption (some Reformed versions) limits the first to the second. Lutherans hold both as the New Testament gives them.

The word is rare in the New Testament. It appears only five times — Romans 4:14, 1 Corinthians 1:17, 1 Corinthians 9:15, 2 Corinthians 9:3, and Philippians 2:7. Four of those uses are non-christological — they describe faith being “made void,” preaching being “would not become useless” or boasting being “made empty.” The fifth use is the christological one: “but emptied himself by taking on the form of a slave, by looking like other men, and by sharing in human nature” (Phil 2:7, NET).
- To deprive of force or significance. Paul does not preach with eloquent words “so that the cross of Christ would not become useless” (1 Cor 1:17, NET).

Second, the kenosis is the pattern of the Christian life. Paul did not write Philippians 2:5–11 as an abstract Christology lesson. He wrote it as an ethic. The passage opens: “You should have the same attitude toward one another that Christ Jesus had,” (Phil 2:5, NET). The Christology grounds the call. The pattern Christ set is the pattern Christians are to live. We are not asked to give up our humanity, or to subtract anything from ourselves. We are asked to add — to humble ourselves, to take the form of servants, to count others more significant than ourselves, to look out for the interests of others rather than our own. The incarnational shape is the shape of Christian discipleship: not diminishment, but humble addition.

“How are they to call on one they have not believed in? And how are they to believe in one they have not heard of? And how are they to hear without someone preaching to them? And how are they to preach unless they are sent...faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the preached word of Christ” (Romans 10:14–15, 17, NET)

*The eschatological inheritance.* Psalm 16:5-6 — “Lord, you give me stability and prosperity; you make my future secure. It is as if I have been given fertile fields or received a beautiful tract of land.” Psalm 73:26 — “My flesh and my heart may grow weak, but God always protects my heart and gives me stability.” The NET expresses the Hebrew portion imagery in terms of stability and security; the inheritance connection concerns the underlying Hebrew vocabulary. The Hebrew psalmists develop the LORD-as-inheritance theme beyond the Levites, applying it to every Israelite who clings to God as his ultimate possession.

*The cosmic dimension — all things in Christ.* Ephesians 1:10-11, 14. The inheritance is not just personal eternal life but participation in the cosmic renewal Christ is bringing about. The believer shares in Christ's inheritance of “all things” (Hebrews 1:2, NET).

*Ephesians 1:11–14.* The NET begins, “In Christ we too have been claimed as God’s own possession,” and later names the Spirit as “the down payment of our inheritance, until the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.” The verb *eklērōthēmen* in verse 11 belongs to the language of allotment. The NET understands it here as God claiming His people as His possession; other grammatical explanations emphasize the inheritance allotted to them. Verse 14 explicitly names the inheritance, *klēronomia*. In either case, God acts first: He claims His people and gives His Spirit as the guarantee of what He has promised.
Paul offers a striking observation about heirs. “Now I mean that the heir, as long as he is a minor, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything” (Galatians 4:1, NET).

*God Himself as the ultimate inheritance.* Beyond the land, the deepest dimension of the Hebrew inheritance tradition is that God Himself is the inheritance of His people. Psalm 16:5-6 — “Lord, you give me stability and prosperity; you make my future secure. It is as if I have been given fertile fields or received a beautiful tract of land.” Psalm 73:26 — “My flesh and my heart may grow weak, but God always protects my heart and gives me stability.” The NET expresses the Hebrew portion imagery in terms of stability and security; the inheritance connection concerns the underlying Hebrew vocabulary. Lamentations 3:24 — “‘My portion is the Lord,’ I have said to myself, so I will put my hope in him.” The believer's ultimate inheritance is not a thing but God Himself.

*The reduction of the inheritance to earthly prosperity.* Some Christianity, especially the prosperity gospel, has effectively reduced the believer’s inheritance to material blessings in the present age — health, wealth, success. The biblical inheritance is different. The believer’s inheritance is “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading. It is reserved in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4, NET). The inheritance is the kingdom, eternal life, the new creation, communion with God — not earthly prosperity. The prosperity reduction misdirects the believer’s hope toward the present age, when the inheritance is fundamentally eschatological.
- The general call of the gospel, addressed to all who hear. “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt 22:14, NET).
“They were devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.” (Acts 2:42, NET)

The Greek word at the center of this question is *krisis* — judgment. The word names the eschatological assessment of all people that accompanies the resurrection: the great and final reckoning at which God judges the living and the dead. The word is not abstract or theoretical; the word names the reality every person will face. And the way the New Testament handles this word — especially in the Gospel of John — gives the resolution to the believer's tension. The believer who is in Christ, John tells us, “not be condemned, but has crossed over from death to life” (John 5:24, NET). The judgment is real; but for the believer in Christ, the judgment has already been faced — and faced by Christ in the believer's place.

The judgment is good news for those who have suffered injustice. The God who judges rightly will vindicate the oppressed, the persecuted, the martyred. The cry of the martyrs under the altar — “before you judge those who live on the earth and avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10, NET) — will be answered at the final judgment. The injustices of history will not stand forever; the righteous Judge will set things right.

The interpretive question for any given verse is: which sense is the speaker using? When Sarah calls Abraham *kyrios* in 1 Peter 3:6, it is the marital-respect sense. When the servants in the parable of the talents address their master as *kyrios* (Matt 25:20), it is the household sense. When Paul writes that there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph 4:5, NET), he means Jesus, and he means it in the fullest sense the word can carry. Context tells you.

*Hosea 1:9-10; 2:23* — the prophetic word about restoration. Hosea's third child is named *Lo-Ammi* — "Not My People" — as a sign of God's judgment on Israel. But the prophetic word includes a reversal: “it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it will be said to them, ‘You are children of the living God” (Hosea 1:10, NET). And in 2:23 — “I will say to ‘Not My People’ (Lo-Ammi), ‘You are my people!’ And he will say, ‘You are my God!’” The prophetic word about Israel's restoration becomes, in the New Testament, the framework for understanding the inclusion of Gentile believers in God's people.
- A single word — the basic sense. “For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matt 12:37, NET). What comes out of your mouth.
- A reckoning or account, in the bookkeeping sense. “Therefore, each of us will give an account of himself to God” (Rom 14:12, NET). The word reaches into the courtroom and the ledger.

- The gospel message itself. “The word of God continued to spread” (Acts 6:7, NET); “Consequently faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the preached word of Christ” (Rom 10:17, NET). When the apostles say *the logos*, with the definite article and no further specification, they often mean the gospel.

The third is the loaded reading of every occurrence. *Logos* shows up some 330 times in the New Testament, and most of those occurrences are ordinary speech: a word, a message, a statement, a saying. Not every *logos* is the eternal Logos. When Jesus says “for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matt 12:37, NET), he is talking about your ordinary words — the things you say at the dinner table and in the parking lot. Context governs. Let the verse around the word do its work.

“was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and our hands have touched (concerning the word of life— and the life was revealed, and we have seen and testify...we have seen and heard we announce to you too, so that you may have fellowship with us (and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:1–3, NET)

The senses overlap in the New Testament's actual usage. A passage may carry several at once. When John writes that “this is the testimony of God that he has testified concerning his Son” (1 John 5:9, NET), *martyria* names both the act (God testifies) and the content (what God testifies — namely, that He has given us eternal life in His Son). Context governs which sense is dominant, and often it is multiple senses at once.

The sentence continues by saying this happened unwillingly, because of the one who subjected it, and in hope. The NET identifies that one as God. The next verse explains the hope: creation will share in the glorious freedom of God's children.

- A principle or pattern. Paul speaks of “the law of sin” (Rom 7:23, 25, NET), “the law of the life-giving Spirit” (Rom 8:2, NET), “the principle of faith” (Rom 3:27, NET) — uses where *nomos* is closer to "rule of operation" than to "commandment."
- The standard of life for Christians. Paul uses “the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2, NET) in this sense — though even here he is contrasting the new pattern with the old Mosaic pattern.

The second is antinomianism — the opposite error. Some readers, having received the gospel of justification by grace through faith apart from works of the law, conclude that the law has no further use for the Christian. Paul anticipates this conclusion and rejects it: “Are we to remain in sin so that grace may increase? Absolutely not!” (Rom 6:1–2, NET). The Christian is freed from the law’s condemnation, not from the law’s instruction. The third use of the law — the law as guide for the Christian life — is what the Formula of Concord, Article VI, defends against the antinomian denial. Even those who have been justified continue to need the law’s instruction, the law’s diagnosis when they fall into sin, and the law’s restraint when they are tempted.

The traditional phrase *rightly dividing* has shaped how many readers hear 2 Timothy 2:15. The NET instead speaks of “teaching the message of truth accurately.” That wording brings the question into focus: what kind of work does *orthotomeō* ask the teacher to do?

*To handle correctly, to deal rightly with.* The extension that most modern translations adopt: *accurately handling* (NASB), *correctly handling* (NIV), *teaching the message of truth accurately* (NET). All of these are attempts to render a metaphor of accurate workmanship without importing a specific trade.

First, regeneration is the Spirit’s work, not the believer’s. Titus 3:5 says that “he saved us”; 1 Peter 1:3 says that “he gave us new birth”; James 1:18 says, “By his sovereign plan he gave us birth through the message of truth.” In John 3:5, Jesus speaks of a person being “born of water and spirit.” These NET passages place the initiative with God. The believer receives the life God gives through His appointed means; regeneration is not an achievement produced by a decision to regenerate oneself.

**παντοκράτωρ** (*pantokratōr*) means *Almighty* or *ruler of all*. The NET often renders it *All-Powerful*. It names God's sovereign power, not merely his ability to accomplish an unusually difficult task.

The passages where *paradosis* is affirmed are equally striking. In 1 Corinthians 11:2, Paul commends the Corinthians “I praise you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions just as I passed them on to you.” A few verses later he introduces his teaching on the Lord's Supper with the formula: “For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you” (1 Corinthians 11:23, NET) — using the *paradosis* vocabulary in its verb form. In 1 Corinthians 15:3-5 he uses the same vocabulary to introduce his summary of the resurrection gospel — “For I passed on to you as of first importance what I also received—that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.” And in 2 Thessalonians 2:15 he writes: “Therefore, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold on to the traditions that we taught you, whether by speech or by letter.”
“Then I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate to be with you forever—” (John 14:16, NET)

*Paratithēmi* (παρατίθημι) — the parent verb, *to place beside*. It carries both an ordinary sense and a technical one. Ordinarily it means to set food before someone (Mark 6:41; Luke 9:16) — the same gesture, a thing placed within reach of another. Technically it means to entrust: “from the one who has been entrusted with much, even more will be asked” (Luke 12:48, NET); Paul and Barnabas *entrusted* the new elders to the Lord (Acts 14:23); Paul *entrusts* his charge to Timothy (1 Timothy 1:18). Most movingly, it is the verb on Jesus' lips at the cross: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” (Luke 23:46, NET), and Peter's counsel to the suffering, who are to *entrust* their souls to a faithful Creator (1 Peter 4:19). To make a *parathēkē* is an act of trust in the one receiving it.

*Paradidōmi* (παραδίδωμι) and *paralambanō* (παραλαμβάνω) — *to hand over* and *to receive*. Not cognates, but the same idea in verb form, and the pair Paul uses for the tradition of the gospel: “I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you” (1 Corinthians 11:23, NET), “I passed on to you as of first importance what I also received” (1 Corinthians 15:3, NET). The Latin translation of *paradidōmi* gives us the word *tradition*, which means, exactly and only, *the thing handed over*.

The Lutheran tradition also rejects date-setting. Christ Himself said: “But as for that day and hour no one knows it—not even the angels in heaven—except the Father alone” (Matt 24:36, NET). Throughout church history, repeated date-setting movements have appeared and failed. The Millerites of the 1840s, the Jehovah’s Witness predictions of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the various end-times prophecy charts of late-twentieth-century American evangelicalism — all have failed because date-setting is itself contrary to Christ’s explicit teaching. The Christian’s posture is not calculation but watchfulness, not prediction but readiness.
“And now, Lord, pay attention to their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your message with great courage,” (Acts 4:29, NET)
“When they had prayed, the place where they were assembled together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak the word of God courageously.” (Acts 4:31, NET)

The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: teach the wandering image. The Greek *planaō* draws on a rich semantic field — wandering stars, wandering sheep, wandering nations (the English word *planet* preserves the root). Walk your students through the universal pattern: “all of us had wandered off like sheep” (Isaiah 53:6, NET); “you were going astray like sheep but now you have turned back to the shepherd and guardian of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25, NET). The pattern of Christian conversion is the wandering sheep returning to the Shepherd, and every believer’s testimony fits it — even when the personal narrative includes no dramatic conversion moment. Your students are returning sheep: they were being led astray, and they have been brought back by the Shepherd’s work.

For pastoral application, the doctrine calls the believer to watchfulness and humility. He himself can be deceived — “deceiving others and being deceived” (2 Timothy 3:13, NET); the Christian who treats his own discernment as infallible has missed the warning. His discernment is real but always humble, submitted to the Word, open to correction by the church’s confession. And his continuing safety is in the Shepherd, not in his own vigilance: the wandering sheep returned because the Shepherd sought him, and the believer’s continuing walk depends on continuing nourishment from Word and Sacrament — the means by which the Shepherd feeds and keeps His sheep.

The third is missing the polemic. Colossians 2 is not a calm devotional reflection. It is a fight. Paul is denying that you need to look anywhere else for divine reality — and the “or else” of his argument is the part most modern readers skip. He warns about “be careful not to allow anyone to captivate you through an empty, deceitful philosophy that is according to human traditions and the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ” (Col 2:8, NET) in the verse just before our key passage. The fullness is in Christ — and so do not be carried off by anyone telling you otherwise. The pastoral force of the doctrine depends on holding the polemic intact.
“(Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive, for the Spirit had not yet been given because Jesus was not yet glorified.)” (John 7:39, NET)

- Wind, the moving of air. Jesus uses this sense in His conversation with Nicodemus: “The wind blows wherever it will, and you hear the sound it makes, but do not know where it comes from and where it is going. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” (John 3:8, NET). The pun is in the Greek; English has to choose one word or the other.

*Ruth* — the most extended Old Testament narrative of a *ger* (Ruth the Moabite) becoming integrated into Israel. Ruth's confession to Naomi — “your people will become my people, and your God will become my God” (Ruth 1:16, NET) — has become the paradigmatic statement of proselyte commitment. Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of David, integrating fully into the people of God.

Catechesis is the substantive formation of the convert in Christian doctrine and life. The Great Commission's “teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:20, NET) names this continuing instruction. The early church developed elaborate catechumenate practices — extended periods of teaching, moral formation, and gradual incorporation into the community — before baptism for adult converts. The Lutheran tradition has continued this catechetical emphasis through Luther's Small and Large Catechisms, which structure ongoing Christian instruction in the foundations of the faith.

*The neglect of intercession.* Some Christianity has effectively reduced prayer to the believer’s own concerns, neglecting intercession for others. The biblical pattern names intercession (*enteuxis*) as a distinct category of Christian prayer and specifies that intercession is to be made “all people” (1 Timothy 2:1, NET). The Christian who prays only for himself and his immediate concerns has neglected one of the four kinds of prayer Paul names.

*The collapse of the believer’s firstborn status into Christ’s.* Some forms of theology (especially in the *theōsis* tradition or in certain charismatic streams) treat the believer’s union with Christ as a sharing in Christ’s actual preeminence — as if the believer becomes a *prōtotokos* in the same sense Christ is. The Lutheran reading distinguishes. The believer becomes a member of “congregation of the firstborn” (Hebrews 12:23, NET) by union with Christ the firstborn — but the believer does not become *the* firstborn. There is one *prōtotokos*; we are His brothers and sisters, sharing His inheritance, never displacing His preeminence.

For Bible study leaders, the application extends to the Christian’s identity. The believer is part of “congregation of the firstborn” (Hebrews 12:23, NET). This is not aspiration but identity: by union with Christ the *prōtotokos*, the believer shares the firstborn’s family status — full membership, full inheritance, full access to the Father. The Christian life is the lived working-out of an identity already given.
“the Word became flesh” (John 1:14, NET)
“I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:18, NET)
- The sphere of human achievement apart from God's gift — confidence “human credentials” (Phil 3:3–4, NET).
- Ethnic descent or biological family — “my people, my fellow countrymen” (Rom 9:3, NET).

The metaphysical foundation for the Real Presence connects back to [Plērōma](/greek/pleroma/) and the *communicatio idiomatum*. Because Christ's human nature shares in the attributes of His divine nature — including the divine attribute of being present wherever God wills to be present — Christ's body can be present wherever Christ Himself is present, including the table at His Supper. The Reformed objection has historically been *finitum non capax infiniti* — the finite cannot contain the infinite. The Lutheran response is that the incarnation itself disproves this principle. The body of the incarnate Christ already contains “all the fullness of deity” (Col 2:9, NET). If Christ's body could contain the infinite at Bethlehem, the same body can be given at any altar where Christ promises to give Himself in His Word.
“She will give birth to a son and you will name him Jesus because he will save his people from their sins.” (Matthew 1:21, NET)
- Physical rescue from danger. Peter sinking on the water: “Lord, save me!” (Matt 14:30, NET). Sailors threatened with shipwreck: hoping to “be saved” (Acts 27:20, 31, NET).

- Healing from sickness. The woman with the flow of blood — “your faith has made you well” (Mark 5:34, NET) — uses *sōzō*, and the meaning in context is “made you well.” The same verb appears in healing accounts across the Gospels, sometimes translated “made well” or “healed” in English but always *sōzō* in Greek.

Second, conscience does not save — Christ does. This is the point that gets lost most easily in popular Christian usage of "conscience." When someone speaks of having "a clean conscience before God," they often mean that they have lived in a way that they themselves approve of. But Paul says even of himself, “For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not acquitted because of this. The one who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor 4:4, NET). Paul's own clean conscience does not justify him before God. Only the Lord's judgment does.

The first is identifying conscience with guilt feelings. A person can feel no guilt and still be guilty of grave sin — Paul calls this conscience “seared” (1 Tim 4:2, NET). A person can feel terrible guilt for things that are not sin — a scrupulous conscience, malformed by bad teaching or psychological wound. The feelings are downstream of the faculty. The Lutheran pastoral tradition is careful to distinguish between the conscience’s witness (which is meaningful) and the conscience’s emotional accompaniment (which may or may not be accurate). The remedy for guilt feelings unattached to actual sin is not more repentance; it is the recovery of an accurate understanding of Scripture and the application of the gospel to the false accusation.
“So then, be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48, NET)

The Hebrew background reinforces this. The Old Testament word the Septuagint frequently translates with *teleios* is *tamim* — “whole, complete, sound, unblemished, blameless.” *Tamim* describes integrity and wholeness, not metaphysical perfection. Noah was *tamim* in his generations (Gen 6:9) — not sinless in the abstract, but whole and blameless in covenant integrity relative to his time. God’s command to Abraham was “Walk before me and be blameless” (Gen 17:1, NET) — not “be metaphysically flawless” but “be whole, complete in covenant relationship.” The Hebrew concept focuses on integrity and wholeness, and the Greek *teleios* picks up this same conceptual world.

The pastoral payoff is concrete. The believer who faces death can take Paul's confidence: “for to me, living is Christ and dying is gain” (Philippians 1:21, NET). The believer who is grieving the death of a brother or sister in Christ has the assurance that the loved one is “with Christ, which is better” (Philippians 1:23, NET). The fear of death — what the writer of Hebrews calls "the slavery" of fearing death (Hebrews 2:15) — is broken in Christ. Not the experience of death, but the slavery of fearing it.

The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: many adults in your class are facing death — their own approaching, their parents’, their spouses’. Teach the Christian view plainly, in four points. *Death is real* — the Christian tradition does not minimize it; grief is appropriate, and the believer at the graveside honors what God has not yet removed. *Death is conquered* — Christ has gone before; the cross has paid the wages and the resurrection broken death’s power, so the believer’s death is not the unbeliever’s. *Death is the passage* — for the believer it is not the wages but the doorway: “to depart and be with Christ, which is better” (Philippians 1:23, NET). *Death awaits final defeat* — the resurrection at the last day will complete what Christ’s resurrection began; the last enemy will be destroyed.

The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: when you teach about God in your adult class, what God are you teaching about? American religious culture defaults toward a “generic theism” — God as a vague benevolent presence, a higher power — and even regular churchgoers carry that default into their hearing of Scripture. When you read “God loved the world” (John 3:16, NET), the word “God” in your students’ ears may default to that generic deity, not to the Father of Jesus Christ who spoke through the prophets and acted in history.

There is exactly one place in the New Testament where the word *theotēs* appears: Colossians 2:9. Paul writes, in Greek: *en autō katoikei pan to plērōma tēs theotētos sōmatikōs*. In the NET: “For in him all the fullness of deity lives in bodily form” (Colossians 2:9).

In Romans 5:14, Paul calls Adam “a type of the coming one” (Romans 5:14, NET). The connection there concerns the action of one man and its consequences for many. Paul identifies the pattern and then explains how Christ's gift surpasses Adam's trespass.
“The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; I have come so that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10, NET)

*Bios* (βίος): the dominant senses are “the course of life,” “livelihood, means of subsistence,” and “way of life.” When Mark records the widow casting in her last two coins, “what she had to live on, everything she had” (Mark 12:44, NET), the word is *bios* — all her livelihood, what she lived on. When Paul tells Timothy to avoid “the affairs of *bios*” so as to please the One who enlisted him (2 Tim 2:4), the word is *bios* — the practical affairs of daily life. *Bios* is the practical, durational, conditional life — the conditions under which biological existence takes place.

*Zōē* (ζωή): the dominant senses are “life as the principle itself,” “vitality,” and “the life God gives.” When John writes that “in him was life” (John 1:4), the word is *zōē* — life as such, the vital principle, what God shares with His creation. When Jesus says “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25, NET), the word is *zōē* — Christ Himself as the life. When Paul writes “Christ (who is your life)” (Col 3:4, NET), the word is *zōē* — the substantive, principial life that Christ Himself is.

curatedProseOverrides.contains: The antinomian error treats the transfer as removing all obligation to the law
curatedProseOverrides.old: This emphasis distinguishes confessional Lutheran teaching from two opposite errors. The antinomian error treats the transfer as removing all obligation to the law — the believer is "free from the law" in a way that exempts him from obedience. The legalistic error treats the transfer as conditional on the believer's continuing performance — the believer's status depends on his ongoing works. Lutheran teaching holds both: the transfer is by grace through faith (against legalism), and the transfer obligates the believer to active obedience (against antinomianism). The Formula of Concord Article VI (on the third use of the law) is the foundational confessional Lutheran treatment of this tension.

curatedProseOverrides.contains: *The antinomian misreading.*
curatedProseOverrides.old: *The antinomian misreading.* Some Christian traditions, especially in popular evangelical Protestantism, have inferred from passages like Romans 6:14 (“you are not under law but under grace”) that the law no longer has any claim on the believer’s conduct. The Christian is “free from the law” in a way that means free from any obligation to its commands. The New Testament will not bear this. Christ redeems us *from* the law’s curse (Galatians 3:13) and *from* slavery to *anomia* (Titus 2:14), but not from the obligation to obedient love of God and neighbor. The Lutheran tradition has consistently resisted antinomianism — most famously in the antinomian controversies of the 1530s and 1540s, which produced the careful treatment of the law in the Formula of Concord.

curatedProseOverrides.contains: The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: teach the doctrine of inspiration.
curatedProseOverrides.old: The Sunday school teacher angle is direct: teach the doctrine of inspiration. Most lay readers know the Bible is “the Word of God” but have not worked through what that means. Walk through two passages. 2 Timothy 3:16 — “Every scripture is inspired by God”; the Greek *theopneustos* names what Scripture *is*: produced by God’s own breath, not merely “deeply moving.” 2 Peter 1:21 — “for no prophecy was ever borne of human impulse; rather, men carried along by the Holy Spirit spoke from God”; the participle *pheromenoi* pictures the authors carried like a ship in the wind. Together they give the full doctrine: Scripture is fully human (real people wrote it, with their own vocabulary and personality) and fully divine (the Spirit carried them, so what they wrote is God’s breathed-out Word). This is what makes *sola Scriptura* coherent — Scripture alone as the norm, because Scripture alone is *theopneustos*.

curatedProseOverrides.contains: The NET renders the opening of the verse:
curatedProseOverrides.old: Romans 3:25 brings several dimensions of the cross together in one Greek word: *hilastērion*. The NET renders the opening of the verse: “God publicly displayed him at his death as the mercy seat accessible through faith.” The phrase *mercy seat* brings the Old Testament place of atonement into view. Other familiar renderings emphasize propitiation, expiation, or a sacrifice of atonement. Those terms direct attention to related questions: how sin is dealt with, how divine judgment is answered, and where God meets sinners in mercy. This study argues that the word’s sacrificial background belongs with the Lutheran confession that Christ bore our sin and God’s judgment against it. That argument must be made from the passage and its biblical context; it should not be made to depend on an English translation printing the word *propitiation*.

curatedProseOverrides.contains: The NET’s “his essence” translates
curatedProseOverrides.old: The substantive use. The NET’s “his essence” translates *tēs hypostaseōs autou* — “his *hypostasis*.” Christ is the *charaktēr* — the exact stamp or imprint, like the impression a seal makes on wax — of God’s *hypostasis*. The image is concrete: Christ bears the imprint of God’s own being in such a way that to see Christ is to see God. Hebrews 1:3 is one of the foundational New Testament texts for the deity of Christ, sitting alongside John 1:1, Philippians 2:6, and Colossians 1:15–20. Christ is not merely a creature who reflects God’s character at a distance; Christ bears the very imprint of the divine being itself. The Greek word *charaktēr* (from which the English “character” descends) was used for the imprint a die makes on a coin — exact, precise, of the same substance as what stamped it. Christ is to God the Father what the imprint on a coin is to the die that stamped it: not a different reality but a precise impression of the same.

curatedProseOverrides.contains: Compare the NET’s “what has been entrusted to me”
curatedProseOverrides.old: *What has been entrusted to God — or to Paul.* 2 Timothy 1:12 is genuinely ambiguous in Greek, and honest translations disagree. Paul writes that he is convinced God is able to guard *tēn parathēkēn mou* — "my deposit" — until that day. A possessive genitive can point either direction. It may mean *the deposit I have made with him*: Paul has handed his life, his work, and his death over to God for safekeeping. It may mean *the deposit he has made with me*: the gospel Paul was given, which God himself will preserve. Compare the NET’s “what has been entrusted to me” with the alternative reading, “what has been entrusted to me.” The direction of the entrusting is an interpretive decision. Both readings are grammatically available and both are theologically sound; the verse is one of the places where a translator has to choose and the reader deserves to be told that a choice was made. The immediate context, where verse 14 clearly means the gospel entrusted to Timothy, gives a mild edge to the second reading. It is an edge, not a proof.

curatedProseOverrides.contains: The connections to the means of grace are direct.

inlineReviewSample.old: What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but does not have works? Can this kind of faith save him? If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, keep warm and eat well,’ but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is it? So also faith, if it does not have works, is dead being by itself. But someone will say, ‘You have faith and I have works.’ Show me your faith without works and I will show you faith by my works. You believe that God is one; well and good. Even the demons believe that—and tremble with fear. But would you like evidence, you empty fellow, that faith without works is useless? Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered Isaac his son on the altar? You see that his faith was working together with his works and his faith was perfected by works. And the scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘Now Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness,’ and he was called God’s friend. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. And similarly, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by another way? For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so also faith without works is dead.
inlineReviewSample.new: What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him? Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you tells him, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that? So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead. But someone will say, “You have faith and I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder. O foolish man, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless? Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did. And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God. As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone. In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.

records.old: But someone will say, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?’ Fool! What you sow will not come to life unless it dies. All flesh is not the same: People have one flesh, animals have another, birds and fish another. And there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. The glory of the heavenly body is one sort and the earthly another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon and another glory of the stars, for star differs from star in glory. It is the same with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.

records.old: What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but does not have works? Can this kind of faith save him? If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, keep warm and eat well,’ but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is it? So also faith, if it does not have works, is dead being by itself. But someone will say, ‘You have faith and I have works.’ Show me your faith without works and I will show you faith by my works. You believe that God is one; well and good. Even the demons believe that—and tremble with fear. But would you like evidence, you empty fellow, that faith without works is useless? Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered Isaac his son on the altar? You see that his faith was working together with his works and his faith was perfected by works. And the scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘Now Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness,’ and he was called God’s friend. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. And similarly, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by another way? For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so also faith without works is dead.
records.new: What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him? Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you tells him, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that? So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead. But someone will say, “You have faith and I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder. O foolish man, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless? Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did. And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God. As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone. In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.

records.old: When the Son of Man comes in his glory and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. All the nations will be assembled before him, and he will separate people one from another like a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will put the sheep on his right and the goats on his left. Then the king will say to those on his right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you invited me in, I was naked and you gave me clothing, I was sick and you took care of me, I was in prison and you visited me.’ Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you something to drink? When did we see you a stranger and invite you in, or naked and clothe you? When did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?’ And the king will answer them, ‘I tell you the truth, just as you did it for one of the least of these brothers or sisters of mine, you did it for me.’ ‘Then he will say to those on his left, ‘Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels! For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink. I was a stranger and you did not receive me as a guest, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.’ Then they too will answer, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not give you whatever you needed?’ Then he will answer them, ‘I tell you the truth, just as you did not do it for one of the least of these, you did not do it for me.’ And these will depart into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.’

Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are already priests who offer the gifts prescribed by the law. The place where they serve is a sketch and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary, just as Moses was warned by God as he was about to complete the tabernacle.
